tagline: Mountain crossings and a relocated town along Tennessee’s eastern corridor
intro: East Tennessee Crossing runs from the Kentucky border at Cumberland Gap to the North Carolina line beyond Del Rio. US 25E carries four lanes through twin tunnel bores beneath Cumberland Gap National Historical Park. Farther south, the byway climbs Clinch Mountain with views across the Great Valley of Tennessee. The Federal Highway Administration lists the 83-mile National Scenic Byway and highlights its mountain views, historic communities and crafts.

The northern crossing has changed substantially since roads first carried motor traffic through the gap. A road built through Cumberland Gap in 1916 joined US 25E and the Dixie Highway system, but its sharp curves contributed to a high accident rate. The National Park Service proposed a tunnel in 1956; widening the surface road would have harmed historic areas of the park. The tunnel opened in 1996, and the original trail through the gap was restored.

From Cumberland Gap, head south through the Tazewell area and over Clinch Mountain to Bean Station. The Clinch crossing was lowered by 200 feet when US 25E was widened to four lanes. Continue across Cherokee Lake to Morristown, then through White Pine to Newport. At Newport, US 25 leads through Del Rio toward the North Carolina border.

moments.title: Abraham Lincoln Library and Museum
moments.text: Lincoln's cane from the night of his assassination is among the objects interpreted at this museum on the Lincoln Memorial University campus in Harrogate. General Oliver O. Howard helped establish the university in Lincoln’s honor on property once occupied by the 700-room Four Seasons Hotel. The hotel had been sold and dismantled after its financial backers collapsed; only its sanitarium remained when the property was purchased for the university. The university received its charter on February 12, 1897, the anniversary of Lincoln’s birth. The collection began with donations from General Oliver O. Howard and his friends.

moments.title: Bean Station
moments.text: Cherokee Lake covers the original Bean Station site, flooded by TVA in 1942. Plans to relocate the community as a planned village failed amid disputes over land and residents’ reluctance to move. TVA used eminent domain and federal court orders to remove residents. The town shifted to the relocated junction of US 25E and US 11W. Bean Station Tavern was taken apart for relocation, but its materials remained in storage. A later proposal to rebuild it was abandoned because the stored materials had deteriorated beyond repair. The present town lies between Clinch Mountain to the north and Cherokee Lake to the south.

moments.title: Crockett Tavern Museum
moments.text: This log cabin was built in the 1950s to represent the tavern John Crockett established in 1794. The modern museum occupies the approximate location of that earlier tavern. The museum project began in 1955, during the peak of the popular enthusiasm for Davy Crockett, and opened in 1958. It commemorates Crockett in Morristown and is operated by the Hamblen County chapter of the Association for the Preservation of Tennessee Antiquities.
